item.title: American Students Shouldn’t Be Guinea Pigs for Chatbots
item.description:
Every time our education secretary, Linda McMahon, goes on TV to talk about the department she vowed to sunset, I’m expecting some fresh nonsense.

McMahon’s Sunday appearance on CNN’s State of the Union to mark the beginning of the school year was a typical under-informed performance from the woman who once referred to A.I. as A1, as in the steak sauce.

An anchor, Dana Bash, asked her a pointed question about A.I. use in K-12 classrooms. Bash explained that while McMahon’s department released guidance encouraging schools to evaluate technology based on effectiveness, the tech is so new and fast moving, it’s impossible to assess learning outcomes. “Are you concerned that students are effectively becoming sort of guinea pigs for chatbots?” Bash inquired.

McMahon answered Bash by referencing a visit she made last year to Alpha School, a private school in Austin, Texas, that was co-founded by an A.I. entrepreneur and where the students spend two hours a day doing personalized learning on screens. “The first couple of hours every day, students really have on headphones,” McMahon said. “They’re in front of their computers. They’re getting their subjects fed to them, with all teachers monitoring what they’re doing. And the beauty of that is that a student almost has a one-on-one tutor.” Bash asked if this was a “proper model,” and McMahon replied: “It’s working wonderfully. And they have been doing it now for a few years,” and it’s “what we have to look at” even though she was “not saying that works everywhere.”

Alpha School’s methods and claims of student success have never been independently studied or verified, and as a private school, it gets to choose its students. The tools Alpha students use include Khan Academy, whose own founder, Sal Khan, has already walked back some earlier, effusive statements about the promise of A.I. in education. “For a lot of students, it was a nonevent,” Khan said, referring to the introduction of the company’s A.I. chatbot, Khanmigo, into public schools.

Last October, after McMahon’s visit, Wired’s Todd Feathers published an article about families who pulled their kids out of another Alpha School campus, some in the middle of the school year, because their academic and social experience was so miserable.

If McMahon were up-to-date on the latest research and reporting on the use of artificial intelligence in K-12 schools, she might not be so credulous about the aggressive use of A.I. If she were paying closer attention, perhaps she would have discovered a study of over 26,000 Chinese students from grades 7-12 that was published in June by the Center for Economic Policy Research.

The economists David Strömberg, Victor Lei and Yanhui Wu found that while A.I. use raised homework scores among students, it lowered “monthly exam scores by 20 percent within six months. High-stakes entrance-exam scores fall by 18 and 24 percent,” with student performance worsening over time. The students with the greatest negative effects on their exam scores appeared to be rushing through their homework by outsourcing to A.I.

It feels as if our educational leaders have abdicated their responsibility to students, teachers, parents and society by allowing Big Tech to more or less dictate national policy on screens in public schools. In an article adapted from the forthcoming book “Coding Kids: Big Tech’s Battle to Remake Public Schools,” my newsroom colleague Natasha Singer outlines the corporate playbook run by Google, Microsoft, Apple and OpenAI:

Tech companies finance national polls and research reports to help make products like A.I. chatbots, and courses like computer science, more urgent priorities for students and school districts. They advocate for new laws to require schools to teach industry-aligned subjects. They sit on committees that help shape learning standards for public school students. They supply or sponsor teacher training and free course materials for students. They fund the National PTA, teachers’ unions and other prominent groups.

Big Tech companies are already embedded in the lives of many Americans, which is why I find it hard to imagine that we are going to succeed in adequately regulating tech in our schools. But it doesn’t have to be this way — there’s a path forward that involves evaluating educational technology, including A.I., in a holistic manner that goes beyond test scores or corporate deliverables.

Natalia Kucirkova, a professor of early childhood and development at the University of Stavanger in Norway, outlines a sensible methodology for greenlighting screen-based activities in her new book, “The Great EdTech Pivot.” Kucirkova thinks that every piece of ed tech should be measured by a model she calls the five Es: efficacy, effectiveness, ethics, equity and environment.

In the United States, we tend to assess ed tech only on efficacy — asking whether it raises test scores or other learning benchmarks. This standard is set by the federal Every Student Succeeds Act, which prioritizes randomized, controlled studies to evaluate any kind of school intervention, not just new technology. We don’t even do a very good job of that, as there are very few high-quality studies of ed tech products, which are often used in classrooms before they are assessed.

But as Kucirkova points out, even good studies (some of which take place in lab settings) cannot account for how teachers will interact with a product, or how students use it in real life. That’s what effectiveness measures: classroom uptake and utility. Ethics is whether a product has been designed to protect a child’s data privacy and whether it has appropriate security features. Equity is whether tools have been created for a diverse student population; environment is whether an ed tech company has sustainability in mind.

The first two Es — efficacy and effectiveness — must be met before school systems even think about the other three; if a tool doesn’t produce results in a real-life setting, it’s pretty worthless. That is why teachers, children and early childhood experts should be part of the creation of educational technology, because they are its user base, and their goals are not about scaling a start-up.

When I talked to Kucirkova last week, I asked her if she thought it was possible to put such a rigorous evaluation system in place in the United States, where much of our ed tech is produced by profit-focused Big Tech companies and retrofitted for educational purposes. She told me that she’s a big believer in making educational technology a public good, with lots of government support, because “the capitalism model is not serving us in many respects.”

While this may seem like an impossible goal, given our current administration’s slashing and burning of funding for educational research, Kucirkova points to a previous technological success story that came from the United States: “Sesame Street.” The show, which delivered an older version of screen-based learning, was funded through a combination of public money and private foundation support. It was created through a collaboration among TV executives, educators and researchers. Meta analyses have found that the show had a positive educational impact in multiple countries around the world.

In Norway, where Kucirkova lives, the government has seriously curtailed the use of A.I. in the country’s schools. Reuters reports that, before the age of 13, A.I. should barely be used in Norway, between 14 and 16, students “can ⁠cautiously adopt tools under teachers’ supervision,” and between 17 and 19, students should “learn to use AI appropriately so that they are prepared for further education and work.”

This seems like a wise middle ground, but parents need to be able to have faith that the approved tools are quality ones. Kucirkova emphasized that Norway is a much more homogenous and high-trust country than the United States.

Despite those very real challenges, I would love to see at least one state in the Union take on the challenge of properly regulating A.I. use in our schools, because every minute of delay is another opportunity for Big Tech to fill the vacuum, and to use our kids’ brains as their training grounds.

I was very glad to see that New York magazine devoted its Aug. 24 cover to the expensive, private-equity infused nightmare that youth sports has become. Caitlin Moscatello does have some solutions. Minnesota is a stand out, where the state’s “network of 250 public rinks serves as the foundation for a nonprofit youth ice-hockey program with more than 60,000 athletes across the state. The entry cost for Minnesota Hockey is low: Most families pay $200 to $400 per season, and in some parts of the state, there’s no fee at all for a player’s first one and equipment is provided for free.” And the proof is in the pudding, as “Minnesota produces more D-I men’s and women’s ice-hockey players than any other state.” If everybody gets to play, the best players will emerge, rather than the people whose parents can pay the most. Read my previous rants about money destroying youth sports here and here.

Feel free to drop me a line about anything here.

item.title: The Pompous Proof of an America in Decline
item.description:
Frank Bruni: Canada, a previously close ally of ours with less than one-eighth of our population and less than one-tenth of our gross domestic product, just made clear that it won’t be bullied by us and has contempt for what we’ve become. Iran makes a daily mockery of our unhinged overlord’s immature predictions of a lickety-split war and premature declarations of an easy-peasy victory. Could President Trump, so obsessed with his potency, be making the United States look any weaker, Bret? Is he the pompous proof that the era of American dominance is done?

Bret Stephens: Wasn’t it Teddy Roosevelt who said, “Speak softly and carry a big stick”? Trump’s presidency, if not his whole life, amounts to an inversion of the phrase.

Frank: As you made wisely and scarily clear in your most recent column, his speaking loudly while carrying a puny strand of spaghetti is more than a national embarrassment. It’s an opening — for Russia, for China, for a world order in which our say and sway are gravely diminished. Is this a phase? Or is it something more profound?

Bret: Trump is putting America in a position that Niccolò Machiavelli warned all princes against: We are hated, but not feared. That’s not just among enemies like Iran or China, whose rulers carefully watch the U.S. for signs of indecision and weakness. It’s also among our closest friends and allies, Canada chief among them. That said, I really do think that this is a phase related to Trump’s unique awfulness, which expires politically on Jan. 20, 2029. I hope Canadians and other allies bear with America through this period of temporary insanity before we regain our bearings, moral as well as political. Or am I too sanguine?

Frank: I desperately want to agree with you, because I love this country and have so often been proud of it and think we’ve done such enormous good and want us to do yet more of it. But in my gut? You’re too sanguine. Trump strikes me not as an aberration who had the luck of flawed opponents, a feckless Democratic Party and a system in which the Electoral College rather than the popular vote decides presidential elections, which is, of course, how he won in 2016. He’s an expression of America’s id and a reflection of its uncorking. He rose as — and because — so many Americans stopped appreciating our blessings and started wallowing in our resentments. He’s the sign that we summited and have begun the descent. That’s my worry, at least, but I’ve always been someone who girds for the absolute worst so that I can be pleasantly surprised when the merely disappointing happens.

Bret: There’s no doubt Trump has taken advantage of something ugly in the American soul: A few years ago, I compared his relationship to the Republican base to that of a burlesque performer who, with one discarded piece of clothing after another, brings out the inner lewdness of an audience. But I also think, or rather know, that Americans disapprove of his presidency by a wide and growing margin; that Democrats are likely to win back one or probably both houses of Congress in November; that most of us treasure the idea of America as a city on a hill, a destination and an ideal.

That’s not gone.

Frank: But if America’s insistently aggrieved citizens can’t agree on who gets to enter and try to prosper in that hilltop city? If different camps have irreconcilably different versions of the America they treasure? That’s what feeds my dread.

Bret: I keep returning to a line in Bill Clinton’s first Inaugural Address: “There is nothing wrong with America that cannot be cured by what is right with America.” I believe in my bones that it’s true. Historically speaking, we’ve been worse (the Jim Crow South), done worse (Japanese internment, the evils committed against Native Americans), messed up worse (the Smoot-Hawley tariff and Neutrality Acts of the 1930s) and even elected worse (James Buchanan, though Trump may be giving our worst president a run for the money).

We’ve even made the exact same mistakes. My son and I are reading Rick Atkinson’s magnificent account of the early years of the American Revolution, “The British Are Coming,” with its description of our failed attempt to conquer Canada in 1775. My guess is that this third attempt of ours (the second came in 1812) to conquer our hardy northern friends will end much the same way.

Frank: While the individual components of the argument you just made are apt and accurate, I have a problem with the whole we’ve-survived-darker-days line of defense that has been trotted out incessantly over the Trump years. It’s too seductive, too convenient, too obvious.

Bret: Obviousness is not necessarily a defect. Sorry, go on.

Frank: We’ve-seen-worse surely says as much about our desire for reassurance as it does about the actual state of play. Also, our present world is different in ways that weaken historical analogies. I mentioned our fractiousness a bit ago; the internet intensifies that, amplifies it, creates warring truths and pollutes the information ecosystem — as little, if anything, before it did.

Bret: I just had the wonderful experience of spending some time in Abilene, Kan., three miles from the middle of nowhere off I-70, at the Eisenhower presidential library, museum and childhood home. On one hand, it brought home the stark contrast between Eisenhower’s kind of Republican presidency and Trump’s. On the other, I was reminded that at the time, a lot of Americans saw the country and its culture in dire straits — and also dismissed the president as an idiot.

Frank: That last reminder is an excellent one. I remember when everyone around me was freaking out about the singular horror of Ronald Reagan. Then about the singular horror of George W. Bush. Now the same people wish fervently that Trump were more like either of those predecessors of his.

That said, I don’t think, 20 years from now, many people beyond the cronies whose net worth Trump quintupled will be nostalgic for him or this wretched chapter of American life.

Bret: I’m sure you’re right. Reagan had unsuspected tenderness. Bush had obvious decency. Trump’s inner life is a mangy hollow.

Can I change the subject to something a little closer to (your) home?

Frank: Does that mean I’ll have a home-field advantage? Then, sure!

Bret: Adam Grant, the organizational psychologist at Penn, has a terrific guest essay in The Times this week on the subject of how to get college students to stop using A.I. to cheat. His message: Returning to blue book exams isn’t enough; students need an ethical education to understand why integrity matters. Since you teach at a university, tell me what does, or doesn’t, work.

Frank: What works best — and his essay also hints at this — is lowering the stakes. I can’t be sure which or how many of my students at Duke cheat. I’m confident that a very large percentage don’t. But I get the sense that the more stressed they feel and the more selective their desired job or graduate school is, the more they feel entitled or even obliged to cheat. There’s a larger context and problem here: We want colleges to be theaters of learning, but they function just as much as theaters of culling. Those are warring, contradictory dynamics. And within that contradiction, cheating flourishes.

Bret: Completely contradictory. And I wish I could tell every undergraduate in America that what future employers will value most is not a high G.PA. — we’re all aware of grade inflation, anyway — but a demonstrated aptitude for hard work and learning from mistakes. I still have a folder with most of my college essays, and they are terrible. I became a better writer because of, not despite, that convoluted, overstuffed prose. I set out to learn from my mistakes, which first required me to make them, then recognize them, finally and most arduously, to improve. Depriving students of that opportunity is one of the chief evils of A.I.

Frank: Agreed. Part of what’s so frustrating is that students really do want to learn to be better writers — I see this in just about all of them — but they feel that a brutally competitive world puts a dangerously high price on mistakes. As a result, many of them do their best to avoid courses that require extensive writing.

Duke pushes back. It, in fact, requires first-year students in its college of arts and sciences to take a writing seminar, but to add a spoonful of sugar to that medicine, Duke lets them choose among surprising, amusing, quirky themes. One such option in recent years? A writing course titled “Dolly Parton for President?”

Bret: Bringing us to the most important, and by far the saddest, news of the week. I’m struck by how hard the news of her death hit me. I remember, as a kid, watching “9 to 5” in a theater and falling for the force of her personality. But it was only when I had kids of my own — particularly my daughters, who are into country music — that I really began to love the songs, like “Jolene” and “Coat of Many Colors,” not just for their musicality but also for their emotional honesty and depth. Also, if you’ve never heard it, watch Parton, with Emmylou Harris and Linda Ronstadt, cover Neil Young’s “After the Gold Rush,” in this 1999 performance on “Late Show With David Letterman.” It’ll bring you to tears.

Frank: Oh, I’ve heard it. Seen it. Misted up during it. But to me and many others, Dolly Parton was so much more than music and movies. What I perhaps appreciated most about her, Bret, was this: I had no idea what her politics were. I barely had guesses. And while keeping them opaque obviously worked to her commercial advantage, minimizing the possibility that she’d anger and estrange any fans, it came to seem a kind of moral statement: We can have pockets of space and periods of grace in which we savor a shared pleasure and put our differences and our rancor on pause. Her performances were that pause, that space, that grace.

Trump's rise was as a direct result of blowback from outrageous overreach by the political left in general, and Democrat leaders in Washington in particular. Woke gave rise to MAGA. It's that simple. Frank intentionally blows right past that.Congresswoman AOC, "oh, that Woke 1 was so crazy ... our bad!"No - it's far worse than that. A totalitarian leftist movement swept over the halls of power, in the universities, media and government, for two decades. Obama's administration is where and when it all came together. And it was terrible for the nation.Trump is in power now because of the insanities of the totalitarian left in the past. Trump continues to have support now, as will his successors, because the middle and right know that as soon as the Democrats win an election we'll be right back to the same insanities.

Bret: Canadians cannot wait until 2029. There is no guarantee that the next President would not be as awful. All Republicans support this awfulness and will enjoy continuing it. Once a trust is gone, it is gone for good. Canadians will never trust a US administration to tie themselves too closely. It is history ..

A few comments here:1. Bret, you are too sanguine. Trump has spent political & diplomatic capital that had been saved up with our Allies. The problem is he spent the capital on the wrong things. The capital isn’t coming back. It’s spent.2. You mention Eisenhower. Eisenhower was right. We are spending $1 trillion annually on defense. Was I know the breakdown of that is a lot of pensions, medical care, etc. But how about we spend a hell-of-a-lot less on defense. Spend it on education including trades, healthcare and childcare. Start to consider our economic power - in terms of consumption - be considered a large part of our defense. The Chinese aren’t going to kill the goose that lays the golden egg.

item.title: Funding Delays Threaten Rollout of Mamdani’s 2-K Program
item.description:
Funding issues and late payments are threatening the rollout of Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s free child care system for 2-year-olds, two weeks before the program is scheduled to begin, day care providers said.

Many early childhood centers have yet to receive funding to buy classroom furniture and basic supplies like pencils and paper, or to pay newly hired teachers and assistants. Without the money, several providers have warned parents that the centers will not open when school starts on Sept. 10.

Because of the delays, city officials had encouraged providers to apply for interest-free bridge loans from the city — not just for 2-K programs but also for 3-K and pre-K programs. But many of those who have applied for the loans say that money has not arrived either, forcing them to take out high-interest personal loans, borrow from relatives and drain their personal savings.

“Yes, they have a 2-K program, but they didn’t set up the infrastructure to make it work,” said Nurita Love, who operates four day care centers in the Bronx and will have four 2-K classes.

Jenna Lyle, a spokeswoman for the mayor, said that the city would be temporarily moving workers from other agencies to the city’s Department of Education, which oversees early childhood programs, to speed up the review and approval of the contracts for day care providers, which has led to the delay in payments.

Ms. Lyle said that the city would also contact the more than 1,100 providers over the coming days to explain how they could receive bridge loans. She added that the department would be rebuilding the early childhood education division, which lost hundreds of employees during the previous administration.

“These delays are unacceptable, and we are going to fix them,” Ms. Lyle said in a statement. “The Mamdani administration is working around the clock to ensure child care providers have the funding they need by the first day of school.”

Providers have diverted money from their private day care programs or made cuts, such as eliminating snacks for children. Some have asked parents to bring crayons, toilet paper and food on the first day of day care.

The monthly expenses at Ms. Love’s centers exceed $320,000, she said. Without city funds, Ms. Love said, she decided to take out a personal loan and a reverse mortgage on her house to pay her employees, utilities and insurance.

“I had no choice,” she said, adding that this had been the most stressful period in her 43 years running day cares.

Mr. Mamdani made universal child care a centerpiece of his campaign, pledging to make New York the first U.S. city to offer free care from infancy to kindergarten. In recent months, Mr. Mamdani has held celebratory news conferences about the addition of 2,000 seats for 2-year-olds this fall, building on the city’s free child care system for 3-K and pre-K.

The backbone of the city’s universal child care system is not the public schools but neighborhood early childhood centers, which enroll a majority of children. Day care operators have long complained that the city does not treat them equally and that reimbursements routinely arrive weeks or months late.

But in interviews with 18 day care owners and administrators, none said they could recall ever being in such a precarious state. Several day care centers have closed in recent weeks. At some sites, employees have not been paid in a month or longer.

Day care owners added that the Department of Education was hard to reach, often failing to return calls and emails about funding or the bridge loans.

The administrators said they had been hopeful that the program would be improved under Mr. Mamdani, given his focus on universal child care and his pledge to run a city that delivered “public excellence.”

Maria Mavrides Calderon, an assistant professor at the Hunter College School of Education and a former education director at a preschool in the city, said she was “deeply concerned that we are expanding a system that was on a very shaky foundation.”

Theresa Hyland, who operates Little Tots Red Wagon, a preschool in Queens that is slated to run a 2-K classroom of 12, said that an Education Department official told her Wednesday that she would have to cover the estimated $90,000 in upfront costs for the class and submit receipts for reimbursement later. Ms. Hyland also said she could not register the students in the department’s internal system.

“I have bailed them out before, but I am not doing it again,” she said of the department, and added that the center would not open if city funding didn’t arrive soon. “It’s an absolute disaster.”

Samantha Peters, who owns a 3-K and pre-K center in Queens that serves 75 children, had planned to tell her employees on Thursday that the center would not open on Sept. 10 because she had no reserves or savings to afford upfront costs. But she said she found a way to stay open at least for September: Her landlord will allow her to postpone the next rent payment of $10,600, and she will ask her employees to apply for temporary unemployment benefits.

“I am worried — I am scared,” Ms. Peters said. “I don’t know what to do.”

In past years, the centers have received 30 percent of their annual contract in a lump sum before the school year starts, the providers said.

The current situation has led to finger-pointing between city agencies. Education department officials have told day care owners that the payments cannot be disbursed until their annual contracts are registered by the Office of the City Comptroller. But the comptroller’s office said the Education Department must first share the contracts for them to be registered.

None of the providers contacted by The New York Times said that their contracts had been registered. The comptroller’s office said that no contracts for the 2-K program had been shared with it.

“The start of the school year is not an unexpected event,” Mark Levine, the city comptroller, said in a statement. “This needs to be fixed immediately.”

In mid-July, the Lucille Rose Day Care Center in Queens, had run out of money when a Department of Education official urged the organization to apply for a bridge loan, saying that the money could be paid out in less than two weeks. The center’s leaders asked for $125,000.

But the loan was not quickly disbursed. Still waiting for the money, they decided to take out a separate loan for about the same amount.

The bridge loan finally arrived in mid-August, but it was for $75,000, said Sonia R. Banks, the chairwoman of the center’s board. The organization now has $31,000 in the bank, not enough to pay all its bills in the coming weeks, as it prepares to welcome 74 students to its 2-K, 3-K and pre-K classes.

Ms. Banks said that the Mamdani administration should have started to prepare the payments and contracts for the early childhood centers at the beginning of the year.

“Under Mamdani, he swears that he is for community day cares,” Ms. Banks said. “Then he needs to show up and fix it.”
